items.t: BP stock advances balance-sheet strategy with Aker BP sale
sum: BP announced the sale of part of its Aker BP holding on Thursday, November 5, 2026, adding a new portfolio action to its balance-sheet repair plan. Ad Hoc News reported the transaction from a bp press release.

BP sold 5% of its 15.9% holding at NOK 311 per share, raising gross proceeds of NOK 9.83 billion, equivalent to USD 1.06 billion. The company retained 68.7 million Aker BP shares, representing an interest of approximately 10.9%, while the remaining holding is subject to a 90-day lock-up with customary exemptions.

BP raised its expectation for full-year 2026 divestment and other proceeds to approximately USD 9 billion, USD 1 billion above its previous guidance. The proceeds from the Aker BP sale are intended to strengthen the balance sheet, keeping debt reduction at the center of the portfolio reshaping effort.

BP stock traded at 6.69 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 18:03 CET on Friday, November 6, 2026, 0.45% below the Xetra close of Thursday, November 5, 2026 at 6.72 euros. That quote was 2.05% below the 6.83-euro Lang & Schwarz quote in the previous report published on November 5 at 17:35 CET, a separate comparison from the Xetra session move.
Investors can monitor the real-time quote of BP stock during the European session.
The FTSE 100 provides the relevant UK market backdrop for BP stock.

BP's next major strategy milestone is scheduled for December 15, when management plans to outline longer-term plans, a capital framework, performance metrics and targets for a simpler, stronger and more valuable business. sum: BP published stronger third-quarter results on Friday, October 30, as higher refining margins, stronger gas marketing and trading, and improved operations lifted underlying earnings. The company will hold an investor question-and-answer session on Wednesday, November 4, at 1pm GMT, according to its investor relations page.
BP stock traded at 7.10 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 10:15 CET on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. Investors can follow the real-time quote of BP stock.

BP reported underlying replacement cost profit of 8.5 billion US dollars for the July-to-September quarter, up from 5.7 billion US dollars in the second quarter. Reported profit attributable to BP shareholders was 4.7 billion US dollars, compared with 3.9 billion US dollars in the prior quarter.

The company said the underlying result benefited mainly from significantly higher realized refining margins and a much stronger gas marketing and trading result. Refining availability improved to 96.5 percent from 94.7 percent in the second quarter, while upstream plant reliability rose to 95.3 percent from 92.4 percent.

Operating cash flow reached 14.8 billion US dollars, about 4.0 billion US dollars above the previous quarter. BP said the increase reflected stronger underlying earnings, partly offset by higher income-tax payments. Net debt fell by 8.4 billion US dollars to 13.9 billion US dollars at the end of September, compared with 22.3 billion US dollars three months earlier.

Management said balance-sheet repair remains its top priority. BP intends to direct excess cash toward its remaining Deepwater Horizon liabilities while protecting the dividend and maintaining disciplined investment. The company also said it has delivered its net-debt and structural-cost-reduction targets ahead of the broader 2027 timetable.

The quarter included 4.0 billion US dollars of impairments, linked largely to transition businesses. BP said it is simplifying the portfolio through asset sales and partnerships, with the expected Castrol divestment still positioned to provide 6 billion US dollars for further balance-sheet strengthening.

sum: (The FINANCIAL) — The BP Castrol sale has closed, delivering $6 billion in after-tax proceeds for debt reduction as investors assess whether exceptional quarterly cash generation can translate into durable shareholder returns.

The previously announced transaction terms included approximately $0.8 billion of prepaid future dividend income on BP’s retained stake. That component matters: some cash received now represents income brought forward, rather than additional recurring earnings. The proceeds should also be distinguished from cash generated by BP’s operations.

BP’s London ordinary shares (LSE: BP.; American depositary shares NYSE: BP) closed November 2 at 600 pence, or £6.00, down 27.40 pence, or 4.37%, from 627.40 pence. BP’s third-quarter SEC filing shows operating cash flow of $14.829 billion, compared with $7.786 billion a year earlier. Capital expenditure was $3.036 billion. Subtracting that expenditure gives $11.793 billion; this is a calculation of operating cash flow less capital expenditure, not an independently reconciled adjusted free-cash-flow measure.

Net debt was $13.870 billion at September 30. The Castrol completion occurred afterward, so the quarter-end balance does not show the transaction’s final effect. Finance debt remained substantially larger, at $55.366 billion. Net debt and gross financing obligations describe different exposures.

sum: BP has picked up fresh backing from two major Wall Street houses, with UBS and Wells Fargo both lifting their price targets on the same day the oil major completed the sale of a majority stake in its lubricants arm. The stock, however, refused to join the party: BP shares were down 2.0% in trading, a reminder that upgraded targets and a stronger balance sheet do not always translate into immediate buying interest.

The Castrol transaction, closed today, hands 65% of the lubricants business to Stonepeak and delivers BP net proceeds of $6 billion after tax. The company intends to direct that money toward debt reduction. BP keeps a 35% stake in the new joint venture and can sell the remainder after a two-year lock-up period. Stonepeak has named former Shell chief executive Ben van Beurden to chair the new Castrol board.

UBS analyst Joshua Stone raised his target to 725 pence from 700 pence while reiterating a buy rating. His case rests as much on operations as on the disposal proceeds: BP beat expectations for a third consecutive quarter in Q3, with adjusted net income running 15% above consensus. That distinction matters for valuation — an asset sale is a one-off cash injection, whereas quarterly results speak to ongoing earning power.

Wells Fargo, for its part, lifted its target to $63 from $57 and kept an overweight rating, arguing that debt reduction opens the door to higher shareholder returns in 2027. The bank pointed to operating cash flow of $14.3 billion in the third quarter of 2026, excluding working capital movements, which came in ahead of its own $12.9 billion estimate.

Those numbers sit alongside the figures BP reported for the quarter: an adjusted replacement cost profit of $8.458 billion, against $2.210 billion in the same period a year earlier, operating cash flow of $14.8 billion, and net debt reduced to $13.9 billion. Reuters reported that BP has already hit its net debt target a year ahead of schedule, with the Castrol proceeds set to reinforce the balance sheet further.

Investors hoping the windfall will flow straight into buybacks or a richer dividend should temper expectations. BP is prioritising the available funds for debt reduction, and the company has made no commitment to extra share repurchases or a higher dividend.

BP attributed the stronger quarter to higher refining margins and improved gas and marketing trading. CNBC reported that BP's refining indicator margin reached $46.7 per barrel in the quarter, while chief executive Meg O'Neill said margins had started to soften as fourth-quarter demand typically declines after the summer driving and holiday period.

The balance sheet is another focus for investors. Operating cash flow reached $28.55 billion in the first nine months, up from $16.89 billion a year earlier, while net debt fell to $13.87 billion from $26.05 billion over the same comparison period. BP also plans to ringfence cash for remaining Deepwater Horizon obligations.

The November 4 session gives management an opportunity to address how long current refining and trading conditions can support earnings, alongside capital allocation and debt reduction. The latest profit figure benefited from an unusually supportive market environment, so the next discussion is likely to center on resilience if margins and commodity prices ease.

sum: BP scheduled its third-quarter results for October 30, 2026, giving investors the next fixed checkpoint for production, debt and impairment charges. The trading statement also projects refining margins of USD 1.90 billion to USD 2.10 billion and throughput of 1,375 to 1,405 thousand barrels per day. These figures are guidance for the third quarter, not reported results.

For the second quarter, BP reported revenue of USD 69.11 billion, operating profit of USD 7.95 billion and net income of USD 4.33 billion. Operating margin was 11.00 percent in that period, compared with 14.00 percent in the first quarter.

BP shares rise as lower debt and stronger refining margins boost outlook
sum: (Oil & Gas 360) – BP shares advanced Tuesday after the British energy company forecast a significant reduction in net debt and stronger third-quarter refining margins, highlighting improved financial performance despite additional impairment charges in its gas and low-carbon energy businesses.

In a trading update ahead of its October 30 earnings release, BP estimated that net debt declined to between $13.5 billion and $14.5 billion at the end of September, compared with $22.3 billion at the end of June. The reduction puts the company ahead of its previously announced debt reduction targets.

BP’s refining indicator margin increased to an estimated $46.70 per barrel during the third quarter, compared with $29.60 in the second quarter and $15.80 a year earlier. Stronger refining economics are expected to contribute an additional $1.9 billion to $2.1 billion in profit from the company’s products business compared with the previous quarter.

The improvement reflects tighter global refined product markets as geopolitical disruptions, including the conflict involving Iran, have affected petroleum supplies and international transportation routes.
BP also expects its natural gas marketing and trading performance to improve significantly from the second quarter, while oil trading results are projected to remain broadly unchanged.

The company estimated third-quarter upstream production between 2.19 million and 2.24 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, compared with approximately 2.20 million barrels per day in the preceding quarter.

Despite the stronger operating outlook, BP warned of additional impairment charges totaling between $3 billion and $4.5 billion, primarily associated with its gas and low-carbon energy businesses. The charges follow earlier write-downs involving renewable energy investments and reflect continued adjustments to the company’s asset portfolio.

Here’s the dividend forecast for BP shares for 2026 and 2027
sum: BP (LSE:BP.) shares have been on quite a rampage as oil & gas prices continue to climb. The energy giant’s market-cap has expanded by almost 30% since January, comfortably outpacing the wider FTSE 100. And with profits exploding and debt tumbling, it isn’t hard to see why.
But what does this all mean for dividends in 2026 and 2027? Let’s take a look at the most recent payout projections from institutional analysts.
As a reminder, BP declares its dividends in US dollars rather than pounds. And right now, City analysts currently expect BP to distribute 33.7 cents per share for 2026, rising to 35.1 cents in 2027.

In terms of growth, those forecasts represent increases of around 2.2% and 6.5%, respectively, from the 33 cents paid last year. And at today’s exchange rate and share price, that translates into a 2027 forward yield of roughly 4.8%.
Compared to the 3.1% payout FTSE 100 index investors are currently earning, it’s a pretty attractive offer. But don’t forget that both forecasts and dividends aren’t guaranteed.

Shareholder payouts are dependent on profits, cash flows and management approval. And if market conditions deteriorate, this prospective yield may never materialise. After all, it wouldn’t be the first time BP announced a dividend cut.
The good news is, the latest figures from BP’s second quarter give plenty of reassurance about its financial prospects.

Is now a good time to consider BP shares?
sum: Largely due to the Iran war, BP (LSE:BP.) shares are now (3 August) changing hands for around a quarter more than they were at the start of the year. Past performance is not indicative of future results. But with the energy giant going through a period of transition, could this rally last? Let’s explore.

Shortly, we will know how BP performed during the three months ended 30 June. However, as is customary, the group’s already provided a high-level overview of its output and, more importantly, its revenue. Therefore, we know the numbers could be quite good.

For example, the price of a barrel of Brent crude averaged $103.85 during the quarter, compared to $81.13 for the previous three months. BP estimates that if this was sustained for a full year, it would add $7.7bn to earnings. Similarly, BP’s refining indicator margin has been $12.70/barrel higher. Annually, that’s worth another $7bn.
On the other hand, a fall in the US Henry Hub gas price looks to have cost the group around $1bn.

Overall, earnings per share could show a marked improvement on the previous three months. However, the problem with investing in the oil and gas sector is that BP’s results could easily have gone in the other direction. And there’s very little the company’s directors could have done about it.
That’s why the investment case rests on how well the group deals with the issues that are within its control. This includes, for example, its borrowings, which are on the high side.

At 31 March, its ratio of net debt (including leases) to equity was 33.4%. By contrast, Shell’s was 23%. BP plans to reduce its net debt to $14bn-$18bn by the end of 2027. At 31 March, it was $25.3bn.

Fresh London Stock Exchange announcements, recent market reports and sector commentary have given investors a series of reference points, from large-cap reporting to AIM fundraising and from retail demand to energy volatility.

The UK market has been trying to separate temporary noise from lasting sector signals. Tariff concerns have not disappeared, but recent trading showed that London can still find support when investors see steadier domestic data and calmer energy moves. That has helped broaden attention beyond a narrow set of global defensives.

Iran-US war causes oil price increase again causing BP and Shell shares to rise
sum: BP and Shell shares climbed on Wednesday as oil extended its rise amid a widening war between the United States and Iran.

Shares in BP (LSE:BP) and Shell (LSE:SHEL) rose again on Wednesday, extending a rally in UK oil majors as crude prices pushed higher on an escalating war between the United States and Iran. The move builds on gains made over the past two trading sessions.

BP shares are trading at 538.2p in late morning dealings on Wednesday, up 1.68% from Tuesday’s close of 529.3p. Shell shares are up 1.74% at 3,310.5p, having closed Tuesday at 3,254p. Both stocks remain below their highs for the year: BP peaked at 609.4p in March and Shell reached 3,758.5p in early June. Both are also well above last year’s lows of 393.3p for BP and roughly 2,554p for Shell.

Oil prices have risen as the conflict between Washington and Tehran, which began at the end of February, shows fresh signs of escalating. US forces completed an 11th consecutive night of air strikes on Iran late on Tuesday, and Brent crude was up as much as 4% on Wednesday, according to CNBC, after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran was “not serious” about peace talks.

The conflict has also spread to shipping lanes. Yemen’s Houthi rebels declared what Reuters described as a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia this week, and two Saudi oil tankers reversed course in the Red Sea on Tuesday after Houthi threats, according to the Insurance Journal. Separately, Reuters reported that vessel crossings through the Strait of Hormuz, which carries about a fifth of the world’s oil and gas, fell further on Tuesday amid lingering security concerns.

This is not the first time the war has driven BP and Shell shares higher. BP’s stock rallied as much as 28% after the conflict began before giving back about a fifth of that gain from its March peak, according to the Telegraph. Oil prices had briefly returned to pre-war levels in June after an interim US-Iran deal reopened the Strait of Hormuz, only for renewed disputes over the waterway to send energy costs spiking again.
Sentiment on the oil majors has turned more constructive since Shell’s second-quarter trading update earlier this month.
